patient.chief_complaint: Progressive left arm stiffness and tremor with slowness of movement over approximately two years
patient.history_present_illness:
Mrs. Dorothea Williams is a 77-year-old left-handed retired librarian who presents to the neurology clinic accompanied by her adult daughter for evaluation of progressive left arm stiffness and tremor. Her daughter first noticed a subtle resting tremor in her mother's left hand approximately two years ago while watching television together; the tremor would appear when her mother's hands were at rest and partially subside when she reached for an object. Over the past 18 months, Mrs. Williams has noticed increasing stiffness in her left arm and shoulder, which she initially attributed to arthritis. She reports that daily tasks requiring fine motor dexterity — handling coins, buttoning garments, and writing — have become notably harder with her dominant left hand. Her handwriting has become progressively smaller and harder to read, requiring her to use large-print labels at the library before she retired. She notes that her left arm does not swing naturally when she walks and that turning requires several steps rather than one smooth pivot. She denies any prior significant falls, though she has felt unsteady twice when turning quickly and has self-limited her walking routes as a result.

Critically, Mrs. Williams has several well-established cardiovascular risk factors: longstanding hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus for over two decades, plus a transient ischemic attack six years ago. Her primary care physician, noting these risk factors alongside her gait changes, raised the possibility of vascular parkinsonism and referred her to neurology. The patient herself is concerned about whether she has had 'small strokes' causing her current difficulties. However, she and her daughter both emphasize that her arm symptoms started asymmetrically on the left — not with any step-wise deterioration or fall episode — and that the tremor is most prominent at rest rather than when walking. She endorses a reduced sense of smell that her daughter first noticed three years ago when Mrs. Williams failed to detect the aroma of food cooking. She also reports longstanding constipation managed with a daily stool softener for approximately three years. Her daughter reports observing a vivid dream-enactment episode approximately 18 months ago in which her mother appeared to be shouting and swinging her arms during sleep. The patient notes no significant cognitive complaints, though formal testing reveals mild inefficiencies. She denies visual hallucinations, urinary incontinence, or orthostatic lightheadedness. She has not been started on any dopaminergic medications to date. Her medication list is reviewed and no dopamine receptor antagonists are identified.

results.title: MDS Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Parkinson's Disease
results.authors: Postuma RB, Berg D, Stern M, et al.
results.key_finding: Absolute exclusion criterion for idiopathic PD includes imaging of the presynaptic dopamine system showing normal binding. An abnormal DaTscan supports a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit consistent with neurodegenerative parkinsonism. Lower-limb predominance for more than 3 years is itself an absolute exclusion criterion for PD.

results.title: Parkinson's Disease is Overdiagnosed Clinically at Baseline in Diagnostically Uncertain Cases: a 3-Year EU Multicenter Study with Repeat (123I)FP-CIT SPECT
results.authors: Marshall VL, Patterson J, Hadley DM, et al.
results.key_finding: DaTscan (123I-FP-CIT SPECT) distinguishes neurodegenerative parkinsonism (abnormal scan) from non-neurodegenerative causes including vascular parkinsonism, drug-induced parkinsonism, and essential tremor (typically normal scan). In vascular parkinsonism specifically, the presynaptic dopaminergic terminals are intact and the DaTscan is generally normal or near-normal.

results.title: Challenges in the Diagnosis of Parkinson's Disease
results.authors: Tolosa E, Garrido A, Scholz SW, Poewe W.
results.key_finding: Vascular parkinsonism presents with lower-body predominant parkinsonism, stepwise course, prominent gait failure, and MRI vascular burden. In contrast, idiopathic PD features asymmetric upper-limb rest tremor, insidious onset, non-motor prodrome (RBD, hyposmia, constipation), and clear levodopa response. DaTscan is typically abnormal in idiopathic PD and neurodegenerative atypical parkinsonism, and typically normal in vascular parkinsonism.

results.title: The 'Swallow Tail' Appearance of the Healthy Nigrosome — A New Accurate Test of Parkinson's Disease
results.authors: Schwarz ST, Afzal M, Morgan PS, et al.
results.key_finding: Loss of the swallow-tail sign (nigrosome-1 visibility on SWI/neuromelanin MRI) is found in Parkinson's disease and neurodegenerative parkinsonism with high sensitivity and specificity. It is absent in healthy controls and in vascular parkinsonism.

Carbidopa-levodopa + hydrochlorothiazide: Mild additive antihypertensive effect; monitor for orthostatic hypotension
Carbidopa-levodopa + metformin: No clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction identified
Carbidopa-levodopa + sitagliptin: No significant interaction; both agents well-tolerated concurrently
Carbidopa-levodopa + aspirin: No pharmacokinetic interaction; aspirin does not affect levodopa absorption
contraindications: Non-selective MAO inhibitors (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) — risk of hypertensive crisis; none currently prescribed

warnings: Carbidopa-levodopa may cause orthostatic hypotension — particularly relevant given concurrent antihypertensives (amlodipine, HCTZ); advise gradual positional changes and monitor standing blood pressure
High-protein meals may reduce levodopa absorption; advise consistent protein intake distribution throughout the day
Somnolence and sudden-onset sleep episodes reported; counsel regarding driving safety
Impulse control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive buying/eating) reported with dopaminergic therapy; monitor at follow-up

Nausea is common at initiation; advise small non-protein snack with each dose; peripheral dopamine antagonists (domperidone, where available) may be used for nausea — avoid central agents (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine)

Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) — higher risk of impulse control disorders and somnolence; use with caution in elderly

No dopamine receptor antagonists identified in current regimen; onset predates any new offending agent

Rest tremor with pill-rolling character, re-emergence pattern, bradykinesia, and rigidity incompatible with pure ET

sequence_constraints.reason: Baseline labs and medication review should precede dopaminergic therapy initiation
Structural MRI to exclude vascular-lacunar burden, NPH, and atypical parkinsonism patterns should precede DaTscan interpretation in a patient with vascular risk factors

critical_actions: Apply MDS 2015 clinical diagnostic criteria: bradykinesia plus unilateral rest tremor and cogwheel rigidity, non-motor PD prodrome (hyposmia, RBD, constipation), no absolute exclusion criteria — clinically established PD

Distinguish upper-body asymmetric rest tremor (idiopathic PD pattern) from lower-body predominant symmetric gait disorder (vascular parkinsonism pattern); the clinical pattern here fits PD not vascular parkinsonism

Order DaTscan as the load-bearing discriminating test: abnormal right putaminal deficit contralateral to the clinically worse left side confirms presynaptic dopaminergic loss, which is not expected in vascular parkinsonism
Recognize that Fazekas grade 2 white-matter changes alone do not establish vascular parkinsonism; the DaTscan, clinical asymmetry, and non-motor prodrome together point to idiopathic PD
Review the full medication list to exclude dopamine receptor antagonists before attributing parkinsonism to a neurodegenerative cause
Initiate carbidopa-levodopa with monitoring for orthostatic hypotension given concurrent antihypertensives; a clear dramatic levodopa response is an additional supportive criterion for idiopathic PD
Refer to movement disorders specialist for ongoing management and advanced therapy planning
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose vascular parkinsonism solely on the basis of white-matter hyperintensities when the DaTscan is abnormal and the clinical pattern is upper-body asymmetric rest tremor — this combination identifies idiopathic PD
Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, or promethazine for nausea in a patient with parkinsonism — these agents block dopamine D2 receptors and will worsen parkinsonism

Do not prescribe typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine) or high-potency atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole) — restrict psychosis pharmacotherapy to quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin if needed
Do not prescribe centrally-acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in a 77-year-old patient — high risk of confusion, urinary retention, and cognitive worsening in the elderly
key_reasoning_points: Vascular parkinsonism and idiopathic PD may coexist in patients with vascular risk factors; MRI white-matter burden alone is insufficient to attribute parkinsonism to vascular disease

The key clinical discriminator: vascular parkinsonism is lower-body predominant, symmetric, and stepwise; idiopathic PD presents with upper-body asymmetric rest tremor and insidious onset — this patient has the PD pattern

DaTscan is the definitive ancillary discriminator: reduced putaminal dopamine transporter uptake (contralateral to the worse side) confirms presynaptic dopaminergic loss in idiopathic PD; vascular parkinsonism does not affect presynaptic dopaminergic terminals and typically yields a normal DaTscan
Non-motor prodromal features (hyposmia, REM sleep behavior disorder, constipation) preceding motor symptoms are characteristic of synucleinopathy and are not explained by vascular disease
Absent left nigrosome-1 swallow-tail sign on SWI MRI is a morphological correlate of substantia nigra dopaminergic neuron loss, consistent with idiopathic PD rather than vascular parkinsonism
Clear and dramatic levodopa response, if demonstrated, is a supportive MDS criterion for PD and is typically poor or absent in vascular parkinsonism
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Parkinson's disease is a clinical diagnosis under the MDS criteria; laboratory testing excludes a mimic when one is suspected.
July 2026 review applied: PD remains a clinical diagnosis; no fixed routine laboratory panel, EEG, ECG, formal autonomic or tilt-table testing is part of the PD diagnostic pathway.

red_herrings.data_point: Multiple vascular risk factors (longstanding hypertension, type 2 diabetes, prior TIA) with Fazekas grade 2 white-matter hyperintensities on MRI
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor the differential strongly toward vascular parkinsonism as the primary cause of parkinsonism
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fazekas grade 2 WMH in a high-vascular-risk patient raises vascular parkinsonism, but the upper-body asymmetric rest tremor, non-motor PD prodrome, and abnormal DaTscan with contralateral right putaminal deficit establish idiopathic PD; the WMH represent cerebrovascular comorbidity, not the cause of the movement disorder
